cells.tense: You're here with what you're tending, and your hands are in it now.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you tend and name the point where it's finished, out loud, before you touch it again.
cells.core:
You set things up and keep them going, and you're doing it in the present, not from memory and not from dread. Whatever's in front of you gets your hands on it until it holds its own weight. When it reaches that point, you hand it off without any drama — letting go is just the next thing that happens, not a loss.

That's a balance, though, and balances cost something to keep. The cost here is staying in the present when part of you would rather get ahead of what's next. If it slips, you feel it in the setup: rushing the frames before the material's ready, or gripping one thing so hard the rest goes uncared for. Choose one thing and say where it's done before you touch it again. Then watch what you do with the moment after.

cells.tense: You're standing at the door of what comes next, and it isn't built yet.
cells.ask: Stop one thing you're holding open and let tomorrow stay blank for a week.
cells.core:
You've moved out ahead of what you're growing. Somewhere in front is a setup where everything holds together, and you're building for that instead of for what's in front of you — so nothing gets to be finished, because finishing waits on a plan you're still writing.

The tell is how you handle what hasn't grown yet. You fill the gaps with structure before the material shows you what it wants. Boxes everywhere, none of them empty. That forfeits the good part, the discovering, because only what's in front of you can be discovered and you're already past it. Stop one thing and let it finish on its own clock. Watch what the freed hour does. A thing grows; it doesn't need the next frame built around it.

cells.tense: You used to be the one setting the pattern, and that door is behind you now.
cells.ask: Start one thing badly, in ten minutes, not part of anything larger.
cells.core:
You know how a thing gets built, what it needs, when it's done — and you're not bringing any of it. The skill is still in you. What stopped is the acting on it, and part of you is still back there, in a place you've already left.

What's gone isn't the know-how. It's the appetite — the standing up, the saying yes before you know where it's going. That doesn't come back by tending harder. It comes back by starting something and being seen doing it. Pick the smallest alive thing, no plan, ten minutes. The point is to move and be visible moving, not to finish. Whatever's behind you doesn't get to set today's pace.

cells.tense: You're already arranging the pattern, and you're talking about it as if it did itself.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that you set it up — and then stop carrying it for one day.
cells.core:
You keep things in order around here. People feel the structure you've made — how the week runs, what happens first, what's safe to lean on — and you talk about it like it's just how things are. The setting-up is running. The fact that it's yours isn't in the frame.

So nobody thanks you and you don't thank yourself, and the work of holding it has no bottom to it. Admitting the hand you have in it isn't credit-seeking. It's what lets something you built stand without you holding it. Say once, in plain words, that you set it up. Then leave it standing, one day, without you holding — because what you built holds.

attempts.check: The Too Much cell implies the person spends their effort on outcomes that haven't arrived, which the record does not support as a fact about their life — a person who tends large living things would rightly object that the work is ongoing and real, that they're not bracing for anything and somebody has to keep it alive. The ask survives that objection, because sorting the grown from the not-yet-grown and stopping one thing is useful whether the looming is real or the situation is simply crowded. The sentence that serves me is 'Care that doesn't exhaust' as a summary — it's mine, it labels, and it goes.
